title: The Guggenheim Bilbao
objective: After this level you can explain how one museum changed a city.
summary: Gehry's 1997 museum used aerospace software and titanium skin. Its crowds gave rise to the 'Bilbao effect', which critic Witold Rybczynski argued rarely repeats.

cards.headline: Can one building turn a city around? Bilbao bet a museum on it.
cards.body: The city of Bilbao grew on iron, steel and shipbuilding, and it went through a severe economic crisis in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1997 it opened a new art museum designed by Frank Gehry, a joint venture of the Guggenheim Foundation and the Basque regional government.

cards.headline: Designed with aerospace software
cards.body: Gehry's curves were mathematically complex, so his team used CATIA, software first built for the aerospace industry, to turn his design into a structure and help the builders. Then the skin. Gehry chose titanium after watching how a sample pinned up outside his office behaved. About 33,000 thin titanium sheets now cover the museum, and they change color with the weather and the light.

cards.headline: The Bilbao effect
cards.body: The museum drew about 20 million visitors in its first 20 years, and the former industrial city became a major tourist destination. People began to talk of a Bilbao effect: the idea that one iconic building can transform a city's fortunes.

cards.headline: The skeptic
cards.body: The critic Witold Rybczynski wasn't convinced. In 2011 he argued that nobody had checked whether eye-catching museum architecture really brings the crowds, and that it doesn't, pointing to museums in Seattle and Denver. His title for it: the Bilbao anomaly. One spectacular success, in other words, doesn't make a rule.

questions.prompt: What did Gehry's team use to turn his complex curves for the Guggenheim Bilbao into a buildable structure?

options.label: CATIA, software first built for aerospace
A single sphere, like Utzon's

options.rationale: The complexity called for CATIA software.

questions.explanation: Because the design was mathematically complex, Gehry's team used CATIA, aerospace software, to design and build it.

questions.prompt: What is the 'Bilbao effect', and what did Witold Rybczynski say about it?

options.label: A titanium finish; he said it fades
options.rationale: The effect is about cities, not metal.

options.label: One building transforming a city; he said it rarely repeats
A tax on tourists; he said it was too high
options.rationale: It names a building's impact on a city.

questions.explanation: The Bilbao effect is the idea that one iconic building can transform a city; Rybczynski argued eye-catching museums don't reliably bring the crowds.

Let daylight into the galleries
